newsitem.title: UK: New government overhauls UK financial regulation.
newsitem.headline: New government overhauls UK financial regulation.

text.p: Finance minister Gordon Brown kept up the new Labour government's cracking pace of reform Tuesday by unveiling sweeping plans to overhaul the regulation of Britain's financial services industry.
In a statement to Parliament, Brown announced plans to transfer responsibility for supervising banks from the Bank of England, the central bank, to a strengthened Securities and Investment Board.

The reform will make the new SIB one of the most powerful institutions in the land, responsible for regulating all banks, securities firms and insurance companies. Howard Davies will step down as deputy governor of the BOE to chair the SIB.

Brown said putting supervision of all branches of Britain's important financial services industry under one roof would bring Britain's regulatory structure closer into line with today's increasingly integrated financial markets.

"It would deliver more effective and more efficient supervision, giving both firms and customers better value for money. This would improve the competitiveness of the sector and create a regulatory regime to meet the challenges of the 21st century," Brown said.

It was the chancellor of the exchequer's second bombshell announcement since Labour's landslide election victory on May 1. One of Brown's first acts was to transfer the Treasury's power for setting interest rates to the Bank of England.

He noted that financial markets had approved of that move, with the result that long-term interest rates had since dropped by a third of a percentage point, and said the overhaul announced on Tuesday would also be well received.

"I am confident that the new arrangements, taken together, will enhance significantly the credibility of UK monetary policy and improve the workings of the financial markets," Brown said. "That means lower long-term interest rates and higher growth and investment," he added.

Brown said it had long been apparent that the current system of regulation, enshrined in the Financial Services Act of 1986, was unwieldy and was not delivering the standard of supervision and investor protection the public had a right to expect.

Scandals such as the mis-selling of personal pensions to hundreds of thousands of people convinced Brown while Labour was in opposition of the need for a total reform of the supervision of the financial services industry, aides said.

Under the current regime, a bank is supervised by the Bank of England. But its stockbroking, asset management, retail financial services advisory arm and unit trusts operation are each supervised by a different agency, they noted.

The chancellor said he would start work immediately on the legislation needed to implement the proposed changes as soon as possible, and said Bank of England Governor Eddie George would be fully involved in the task.
Opposition Liberal Democrat members of Parliament welcomed the reform, but Conservatives complained it was hasty and ill thought-out.
